claim: Several Homo sapiens populations experienced admixture with extinct human species during their evolutionary history.
source: It is well established that several Homo sapiens populations experienced admixture with extinct human species during their evolutionary history.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: People belonging to non-African populations show 1–2% of Neanderthal ancestry.
source: In fact, people belonging to non-African populations show 1–2% of Neanderthal ancestry (Green et al., 2010; Prüfer et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 2010 and Prüfer et al., 2014

claim: Melanesians present 3% of Denisovan ancestry.
source: while Melanesians and East-Asians present 3% and 0.2% of Denisovan ancestry, respectively (Reich et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2013; Prüfer et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Reich et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2013; Prüfer et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2017

claim: East-Asians present 0.2% of Denisovan ancestry.
source: while Melanesians and East-Asians present 3% and 0.2% of Denisovan ancestry, respectively (Reich et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2013; Prüfer et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Reich et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2013; Prüfer et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2017

claim: Evidence supporting selection against introgressed alleles has been collected.
source: Despite evidence supporting selection against introgressed alleles has been collected (Simonti et al., 2016; Racimo et al., 2017; McArthur et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Simonti et al., 2016; Racimo et al., 2017; McArthur et al., 2021

claim: Some genomic segments showing signatures ascribable to archaic introgression were targeted by natural selection in modern human populations.
source: some of the genomic segments showing signatures ascribable to archaic introgression were also proved to have been targeted by natural selection in modern human populations, thus providing examples for the occurrence of adaptive introgression (AI) events (Racimo et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Racimo et al., 2017

claim: Introgressed archaic alleles at high frequency have been identified in human genes involved in metabolism or in the response to environmental conditions such as temperature, sunlight, and altitude.
source: So far, several studies have indeed identified introgressed archaic alleles at high frequency in human genes involved in metabolism or in the response to environmental conditions, such as temperature, sunlight, and altitude (Prüfer et al., 2014; Vernot and Akey, 2014; Sankararaman et al., 2014; Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Gittelman et al., 2016; Racimo et al., 2017; Enard and Petrov, 2018; Dannemann and Racimo, 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Some genes that play a role in immune responses to pathogens are characterized by patterns of variability consistent with archaic introgression.
source: Moreover, some genes that play a role in immune responses to pathogens are found to be characterized by a similar pattern of variability (Laurent et al., 2011; Enard and Petrov, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Laurent et al., 2011 and Enard and Petrov, 2018

claim: Certain Neanderthal alleles have been shown to be associated with down-regulation of gene expression in brain and testes.
source: certain Neanderthal alleles have been shown to be associated with down-regulation of gene expression in brain and testes (McCoy et al., 2017; Racimo et al., 2017; Dannemann and Racimo, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to McCoy et al., 2017; Racimo et al., 2017; Dannemann and Racimo, 2018

claim: Admixture provides a very rapid opportunity for natural selection to act on a population's gene pool.
source: By introducing new alleles in the gene pool of a given population, admixture in fact provides a very rapid opportunity for natural selection to act on it (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Jeong et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2015; Hamid et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Jeong et al., 2014; Racimo et al., 2015; Hamid et al., 2021

claim: Gene flow from extinct Hominin species could have facilitated the adaptation of H. sapiens populations to peculiar Eurasian environments.
source: According to this view, gene flow from extinct Hominin species could have facilitated the adaptation of H. sapiens populations to peculiar Eurasian environments.
evidence: Inferred from the context of admixture and adaptation discussion

claim: The adaptive EPAS1 haplotype has a Denisovan origin.
source: For instance, a Denisovan origin of the adaptive EPAS1 haplotype, which confers reduced susceptibility to chronic mountain sickness to Tibetan and Sherpa highlanders (Beall, 2007; Bigham et al., 2010; Yi et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) is well established (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014 and Zhang et al., 2021

claim: The adaptive EPAS1 haplotype confers reduced susceptibility to chronic mountain sickness to Tibetan and Sherpa highlanders.
source: For instance, a Denisovan origin of the adaptive EPAS1 haplotype, which confers reduced susceptibility to chronic mountain sickness to Tibetan and Sherpa highlanders (Beall, 2007; Bigham et al., 2010; Yi et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) is well established (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Beall, 2007; Bigham et al., 2010; Yi et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011

claim: The hard selective sweep experienced by the EPAS1 introgressed haplotype accounts only for an indirect aspect of the adaptive phenotype of high-altitude Himalayan populations.
source: However, the hard selective sweep experienced in high-altitude Himalayan populations by the EPAS1 introgressed haplotype has been demonstrated to account only for an indirect aspect of their adaptive phenotype, which does not explain most of the physiological adjustments they evolved to cope with hypobaric hypoxia (Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2018

claim: After quality control filtering, the dataset comprised 27 individuals of Tibetan ancestry characterized for 6,921,628 single-nucleotide variants.
source: After quality control (QC) filtering of the available WGS data, we obtained a dataset made up of 27 individuals of Tibetan ancestry characterized for 6,921,628 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs)
evidence: Describes the data processing results from the study

claim: The extended dataset including merged WGS and genotyping data contained 231,947 SNVs.
source: We thus obtained an extended dataset including 231,947 SNVs (Supplementary file 1a), which was used to perform population structure analyses.
evidence: Describes the merged dataset composition

claim: Results from ADMIXTURE and principal components analysis were concordant with those described in previous studies.
source: Results from ADMIXTURE and principal components analysis (PCA) were found to be concordant with those described in previous studies (Jeong et al., 2014; Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2017; Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and comparison with current results

claim: The ADMIXTURE model showing the best predictive accuracy was K = 7.
source: According to the ADMIXTURE model showing the best predictive accuracy (K = 7) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by ADMIXTURE analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The examined WGS exhibited a predominant genetic component that was appreciably represented also in other populations speaking Tibeto-Burman languages.
source: the examined WGS exhibited a predominant genetic component that was appreciably represented also in other populations speaking Tibeto-Burman languages, such as Tu, Yizu, Naxi, Lahu, and Sherpa (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by ADMIXTURE results shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The predominant genetic component reached an average proportion of around 78% in individuals of Tibetan ancestry from Nepal included in the extended dataset.
source: Such a component reached an average proportion of around 78% in individuals of Tibetan ancestry from Nepal included in the extended dataset, as well as of more than 80% in the subjects under investigation, who live in the Nepalese regions of Mustang and Ghorka (Figure 1A, B)
evidence: Supported by ADMIXTURE results shown in Figure 1A, B

claim: The predominant genetic component reached more than 80% in the subjects under investigation who live in the Nepalese regions of Mustang and Ghorka.
source: Such a component reached an average proportion of around 78% in individuals of Tibetan ancestry from Nepal included in the extended dataset, as well as of more than 80% in the subjects under investigation, who live in the Nepalese regions of Mustang and Ghorka (Figure 1A, B)
evidence: Supported by ADMIXTURE results shown in Figure 1A, B

claim: Communities in Nepalese high-altitude valleys might have experienced a higher degree of isolation and genetic drift with respect to populations still settled on the Tibetan Plateau.
source: This suggests that after their relatively recent migration in Nepalese high-altitude valleys, these communities might have experienced a higher degree of isolation and genetic drift with respect to populations that are still settled on the Tibetan Plateau, in which the same ancestry fraction did not exceed 64% (Figure 1A, B)
evidence: Inferred from ADMIXTURE results comparing Nepalese and Tibetan Plateau populations

claim: PCA pointed to the expected divergence of Tibetan and Sherpa high-altitude groups from the cline of genomic variation of East-Asian lowland populations.
source: Similarly, PCA pointed to the expected divergence of Tibetan and Sherpa high-altitude groups from the cline of genomic variation of East-Asian lowland populations (Abdulla et al., 2009; Jeong et al., 2014; Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2022; Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by PCA results shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies

claim: The WGS under investigation clustered within the bulk of genome-wide data generated for other groups from the Tibetan Plateau.
source: Remarkably, the WGS under investigation clustered within the bulk of genome-wide data generated for other groups from the Tibetan Plateau, thus supporting their representativeness as concerns the overall genetic background of high-altitude Himalayan populations.
evidence: Supported by PCA clustering results

claim: The study was able to recapitulate the AI event previously described for the EPAS1 gene.
source: According to such an approach, we were first able to recapitulate the AI event previously described for the EPAS1 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies

claim: The EPAS1 chromosomal interval was characterized by a remarkable number of variants (N = 19) showing significant LR scores.
source: In fact, this chromosomal interval was found to be characterized by a remarkable number of variants (N = 19) showing significant LR scores, as well as by high overall values of −logα (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Five significant SNVs at EPAS1 have been already described as Denisovan-like derived alleles at outstanding frequency in Tibetans but not in other modern human populations.
source: Five of these significant SNVs have been already described as Denisovan-like derived alleles at outstanding frequency (i.e., ranging between 0.96 and 1) in Tibetans but not in other modern human populations (Supplementary file 1c; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021 and reference to Supplementary file 1c

claim: At the EGLN1 genomic region, high −logα values were detected coupled with a low number of SNVs (N = 3) showing significant LR scores.
source: On the contrary, at the genomic region encompassing EGLN1 (which we have considered as a negative control for AI, see Materials and methods) we detected high −logα values coupled with a low number of SNVs (N = 3) showing significant LR scores, with only one being remarkably above the adopted significance threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1d)
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Both EPAS1 and EGLN1 loci have been suggested to have adaptively evolved in high-altitude Himalayan populations.
source: Overall, these findings are concordant with evidence from literature that suggest adaptive evolution of both EPAS1 and EGLN1 loci in high-altitude Himalayan populations (Yang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2017 and Liu et al., 2022

claim: Only EPAS1 was proved to have been impacted by archaic introgression, not EGLN1.
source: although only the former was proved to have been impacted by archaic introgression (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021

claim: The study confirmed introgression signatures previously inferred for the PRKCE gene and the MIRLET7BHG long non-coding region.
source: Moreover, we were able to confirm other introgression signatures previously inferred from WGS data for populations of Tibetan ancestry, such as those involving the PRKCE gene and the MIRLET7BHG long non-coding region, which are located in the overlapping upstream chromosomal intervals, respectively, of EPAS1 and PPARA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B)
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: PPARA has been proposed to play a role in the modulation of high-altitude adaptation of Himalayan human groups.
source: In line with what reported for EPAS1, also PPARA has been already proposed to play a role in the modulation of high-altitude adaptation of Himalayan human groups (Simonson et al., 2010; Horscroft et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Simonson et al., 2010; Horscroft et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021

claim: AI signatures identified by VolcanoFinder in the MIRLET7BHG locus extended also in the PPARA gene and its downstream region.
source: Interestingly, AI signatures identified by VolcanoFinder in the MIRLET7BHG locus extended also in the PPARA gene, as well in its downstream region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), supporting the findings described by Hu et al., 2017
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and citation to Hu et al., 2017

claim: The study observed patterns comparable to those at EPAS1 and PPARA for 10 additional genomic regions previously identified as potentially carrying introgressed Denisovan alleles.
source: Finally, we observed patterns comparable to those at EPAS1 and PPARA for 10 additional genomic regions that were differentially pointed out by previous studies as Tibetan and/or Han Chinese DNA segments potentially carrying introgressed Denisovan alleles (Hu et al., 2017; Browning et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021; Figure 2A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1e)
evidence: Supported by VolcanoFinder results shown in figures and citations to previous studies

claim: Six gene networks were identified that were consistently significant across all Signet runs performed.
source: After having crosschecked results from the VolcanoFinder and Signet analyses, we identified six gene networks that turned out to be consistently significant across all the Signet runs performed and that included a total of 15 genes pointed by VolcanoFinder as candidate AI loci (Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results

claim: Four candidate AI loci composed the gene network ascribable to the Pathways in Cancer biological functions, which included EPAS1.
source: Four of these loci composed the gene network overall ascribable to the Pathways in Cancer biological functions, which included also the EPAS1 positive control for AI (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results shown in Figure 3A

claim: Most of the other genes supported by both analyses were observed in significant networks belonging to the Ras signalling and AMPK signalling pathways.
source: Most of the other genes supported by both the analyses were instead observed in significant networks belonging to the Ras signalling and AMPK signalling pathways (Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results

claim: Gene networks belonging to the Pathways in Cancer and Ras signalling pathway are tightly related from a functional perspective because they include oncogenes that promote tumor growth by stimulating cell proliferation and angiogenesis.
source: Interestingly, gene networks belonging to the Pathways in Cancer and Ras signalling pathway appeared to be tightly related from a functional perspective because included oncogenes that promote the initiation and progression of tumour growth by stimulating cell proliferation and angiogenesis (Kranenburg et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kranenburg et al., 2004 and functional pathway analysis

claim: KRAS and RASGRF2 genes from the Ras signalling network contribute to the Pathways in Cancer functions.
source: In particular, according to the Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database KRAS and RASGRF2 genes from the Ras signalling network were found to contribute also to the Pathways in Cancer functions (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by KEGG database information and shown in Figure 3A

claim: KRAS and RASGRF2 interact with identified candidate introgressed loci to modulate the VEGF signalling pathway.
source: especially by interacting with the identified candidate introgressed loci PLCB1, RASGRP2, DAPK1, MAPK1, FOS, and VEGFA to modulate the VEGF signalling pathway, which is activated in hypoxic conditions and induces the transcription of genes that promote angiogenesis (Figure 3A; Maxwell and Ratcliffe, 2002; Kranenburg et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A and citations to Maxwell and Ratcliffe, 2002; Kranenburg et al., 2004

claim: The VEGF signalling pathway is activated in hypoxic conditions and induces the transcription of genes that promote angiogenesis.
source: to modulate the VEGF signalling pathway, which is activated in hypoxic conditions and induces the transcription of genes that promote angiogenesis (Figure 3A; Maxwell and Ratcliffe, 2002; Kranenburg et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Maxwell and Ratcliffe, 2002; Kranenburg et al., 2004

claim: The AMPK signalling pathway is activated in different cell types by stresses such as deprivation of oxygen and/or glucose.
source: Also, the AMPK signalling pathway is known to be activated in different cell types by stresses such as deprivation of oxygen and/or glucose, leading to the inhibition of energy-consuming biosynthetic pathways (e.g., protein and glycogen synthesis) and to the activation of ATP-producing catabolic pathways, such as fatty acid oxidation and glycolysis (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000; Chen et al., 2018; Dengler, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kanehisa and Goto, 2000; Chen et al., 2018; Dengler, 2020

claim: No significant gene networks involving the EGLN1 genomic region were reconstructed with the Signet approach.
source: No significant gene networks involving the EGLN1 genomic region considered as a negative control for AI were instead reconstructed with the Signet approach (Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results

claim: The very few variants at EGLN1 that showed VolcanoFinder LR scores above the significant threshold might represent false positive results.
source: suggesting that the very few variants at this locus that showed VolcanoFinder LR scores above the adopted significant threshold might represent false positive results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1d)
evidence: Inferred from the lack of Signet support and VolcanoFinder results

claim: LASSI analysis confirmed the strong selective events occurred at the EPAS1 and EGLN1 genes.
source: This enabled us to confirm the strong selective events occurred at the EPAS1 and EGLN1 genes, as previously reported by multiple studies conducted on high-altitude Himalayan populations (Beall et al., 2010; Yi et al., 2010; Simonson et al., 2010; Horscroft et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by LASSI analysis results and citations to previous studies

claim: LASSI analysis corroborated adaptive evolution of some genes pointed out by both VolcanoFinder and Signet analyses.
source: as well as to corroborate adaptive evolution of some of the genes pointed out by both VolcanoFinder and Signet analyses. In fact, several chromosomal intervals associated to these loci presented values of the computed T statistic that fall within the top 5% of the related distribution (Figure 4C, D, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2C, D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, D)
evidence: Supported by LASSI analysis results shown in figures

claim: Genomic windows associated to DAPK1, GNG7, AK5, TBC1D1, PLCB1, RASGRF2, and PRKAG2 introgressed loci presented scores within the top 5% of the T distribution.
source: More in detail, in addition to EPAS1, genomic windows associated to the DAPK1, GNG7, AK5, TBC1D1, PLCB1, RASGRF2, and PRKAG2 introgressed loci supported by both VolcanoFinder and Signet approaches were found to present scores within the top 5% of the T distribution, suggesting that their haplotype diversity was appreciably shaped by positive selection
evidence: Supported by LASSI analysis results

claim: Adaptive evolution of the TBC1D1 and RASGRF2 genes has been previously proposed by studies conducted on different populations of Tibetan ancestry.
source: Interestingly, adaptive evolution of the TBC1D1 and RASGRF2 genes has been previously proposed by studies conducted on different populations of Tibetan ancestry (Peng et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to Peng et al., 2011 and Zheng et al., 2023

claim: TBC1D1, RASGRF2, PRKAG2, and KRAS present substantial proportions of Tibetan haplotypes that cluster close to the Denisovan sequence.
source: Among the tested putative AI loci, TBC1D1, RASGRF2, PRKAG2, and KRAS were found to present substantial proportions of Tibetan haplotypes that cluster close to the Denisovan sequence, thus showing the lowest numbers of pairwise differences with respect to it as compared with CHB or YRI haplotypes (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B)
evidence: Supported by Haplostrip analysis results shown in figures

claim: 61% of the TBC1D1 Tibetan haplotypes were the nearest ones to the archaic sequence by entailing only two pairwise differences with respect to it.
source: More in detail, 61% of the TBC1D1 Tibetan haplotypes turned out to be the nearest ones to the archaic sequence by entailing only two pairwise differences with respect to it (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by Haplostrip analysis results shown in Figure 4A

claim: 29% of Tibetan haplotypes inferred for the RASGRF2 gene were identical to the Denisovan DNA.
source: while 29% of Tibetan haplotypes inferred for the RASGRF2 gene were even identical to the Denisovan DNA (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by Haplostrip analysis results shown in Figure 4B

claim: TBC1D1 and RASGRF2 chromosomal intervals were classified by LASSI as regions whose variation pattern conformed with the soft selective sweep model.
source: Interestingly, both these chromosomal intervals were classified by the LASSI method as regions whose variation pattern was conformed with the soft selective sweep model, presenting three potential adaptive haplotypes (i.e., those haplotypes that plausibly carry putative advantageous alleles and thus increased in frequency due to positive selection)
evidence: Supported by LASSI analysis results

claim: At TBC1D1 and RASGRF2, one of the adaptive haplotypes was found to contain Denisovan-like derived alleles that are completely absent in YRI.
source: At each gene, one of these haplotypes was found to contain the Denisovan-like derived alleles that are completely absent in YRI (Figure 4A, D)
evidence: Supported by haplotype analysis results shown in Figure 4A, D

claim: A similar pattern to TBC1D1 and RASGRF2 was observed also for the considered PRKAG2 and KRAS genomic windows.
source: A similar pattern was observed also for the considered PRKAG2 and KRAS genomic windows (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B)
evidence: Supported by haplotype analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: The distribution of similarities between modern and archaic haplotypes for TBC1D1, RASGRF2, PRKAG2, and KRAS is comparable to that observed for EPAS1.
source: Overall, the distribution of similarities between modern and archaic haplotypes described for the four identified AI candidate loci appears to be comparable to that obtained for EPAS1, with the sole relevant distinction being represented by an even more pronounced differentiation between Tibetan and CHB patterns plausibly ascribable to the occurrence of a hard (rather than soft) selective sweep at EPAS1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Supported by comparison of haplotype analysis results shown in figures

claim: At EPAS1, the haplotype carrying the lowest number of pairwise differences with respect to the archaic one belongs to the Tibetan population and reached 74% of frequency.
source: In fact, at EPAS1 the haplotype carrying the lowest number of pairwise differences (N = 3) with respect to the archaic one belongs to the Tibetan population, in which it reached 74% of frequency, being instead absent in all the others modern groups considered (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Supported by haplotype analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A

claim: The EGLN1 genomic window showing the highest T score was characterized by an opposite pattern to EPAS1, with CHB haplotypes being overrepresented among those with the lowest number of pairwise differences with respect to the Denisovan genome.
source: Conversely, the EGLN1 genomic window showing the highest T score according to LASSI analysis was characterized by an opposite pattern, with CHB haplotypes being overrepresented among those with the lowest number of pairwise differences (N = 3) with respect to the Denisovan genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by haplotype analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B

claim: The sole EGLN1 putative adaptive haplotype inferred by LASSI for Tibetans was among those presenting the highest number of differences with the archaic sequence.
source: Moreover, the sole EGLN1 putative adaptive haplotype inferred by LASSI for Tibetans was among those presenting the highest number of differences as compared with the archaic sequence, being characterized exclusively by alleles that are not observed in the Denisovan genome and thus suggesting that natural selection targeted modern rather than archaic EGLN1 variation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by haplotype analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B

claim: PPARA encodes for a nuclear transcription factor whose decreased expression in the myocardium of rats exposed to hypoxia contributes to the maintenance of correct heart contractile function.
source: Interestingly, PPARA encodes for a nuclear transcription factor whose decreased expression in the myocardium of rats exposed to hypoxia seems to contribute to the maintenance of the correct heart contractile function despite such a stressful condition (Cole et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cole et al., 2016

claim: The PRKCE protein kinase C has been demonstrated to exert a cardio-protective role against ischemic injury.
source: Similarly, the PRKCE protein kinase C has been demonstrated to exert a cardio-protective role against ischemic injury (Scruggs et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Scruggs et al., 2016

claim: TBC1D1 encodes for a protein whose serine phosphorylation sites are targeted by AMP-activated protein kinases after the activation of the AMPK signalling pathway.
source: Moreover, TBC1D1 encodes for a protein whose serine phosphorylation sites are targeted by AMP-activated protein kinases (AMPK) after the activation of the AMPK signalling pathway as a result of the increase cellular AMP/ATP ratio caused by stresses that induce a lower ATP production (e.g., deprivation of oxygen and/or glucose) or that accelerate ATP consumption (e.g., intense muscle contraction) (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000; Vichaiwong et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kanehisa and Goto, 2000 and Vichaiwong et al., 2010

claim: Mutations at PRKAG2 are known to cause the PRKAG2 cardiac syndrome, an inherited disease characterized by ventricular pre-excitation, supraventricular arrhythmias, and cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Mutations at this locus are known to cause the PRKAG2 cardiac syndrome, an inherited disease characterized by ventricular pre-excitation, supraventricular arrhythmias, and cardiac hypertrophy (Zhang et al., 2013; Porto et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2013 and Porto et al., 2016

claim: Dysregulation of AMPK activity mediated by reduction in PRKAG2 expression leading to impairment of glycogen metabolism has been proposed as a possible cause for the development of PRKAG2 cardiac syndrome.
source: Dysregulation of AMPK activity mediated by reduction in PRKAG2 expression and leading to the impairment of glycogen metabolism in cell cultures has been proposed as a possible cause for the development of this pathological condition (Zhang et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013

claim: Enhanced activation of the AMPK signalling pathway during pregnancy coupled with PRKAG2 overexpression was observed in the placenta of women living at high altitudes compared with women living in low-altitude regions.
source: Conversely, enhanced activation of the AMPK signalling pathway during pregnancy coupled with PRKAG2 overexpression was observed in the placenta of women living at high altitudes when compared with women living in low-altitude regions (Lorca et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorca et al., 2021

claim: High-altitude individuals of Tibetan ancestry exhibit reduced incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events with respect to low-altitude controls.
source: Finally, high-altitude individuals of Tibetan ancestry were found to exhibit reduced incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events with respect to low-altitude controls possibly indicating the involvement of protective cardiac mechanisms in the modulation of high-altitude adaptations as previously proposed (Kolár and Ostádal, 2004; Mallet et al., 2018; Lei et al., 2024)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kolár and Ostádal, 2004; Mallet et al., 2018; Lei et al., 2024

claim: Adaptive evolution at PPARA, PRKCE, TBC1D1, and PRKAG2 genomic regions in Tibetans might have contributed to the development of protective mechanisms that reduce cardiovascular risk associated to hypoxic stress.
source: We can thus speculate that adaptive evolution at the PPARA, PRKCE, TBC1D1, and PRKAG2 genomic regions in Tibetans might have contributed to the development of protective mechanisms that reduce cardiovascular risk associated to the hypoxic stress.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the functional roles of these genes and their adaptive evolution

claim: RASGRF2 and KRAS have been previously proved to have been targeted by natural selection in Tibetan populations or to present putative introgressed archaic alleles.
source: In addition to these genes, other two of the identified candidate AI loci (i.e., RASGRF2 and KRAS) have been previously proved to have been targeted by natural selection in Tibetan populations (Peng et al., 2011) or to present putative introgressed archaic alleles (Hu et al., 2017; Browning et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4)
evidence: Supported by citations to Peng et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2017; Browning et al., 2018

claim: The Ras protein specific guanine nucleotide releasing factor 2 is a calcium-regulated nucleotide exchange factor that activates the RAS protein codified by the proto-oncogene KRAS.
source: The proteins encoded by these loci are strictly related from a functional perspective, with the Ras protein specific guanine nucleotide releasing factor 2 representing a calcium-regulated nucleotide exchange factor that activates the RAS protein codified by the proto-oncogene KRAS (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000; Sayers et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kanehisa and Goto, 2000 and Sayers et al., 2022

claim: TBC1D1 and PRKAG2 are included in a significant gene network belonging to the AMPK signalling pathway.
source: Archaic introgression at these genomic regions was first confirmed by Signet analysis, with TBC1D1 and PRKAG2 being included in a significant gene network belonging to the AMPK signalling pathway, while RASGRF2 and KRAS participate to that related to the Ras signalling pathway (Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results

claim: RASGRF2 and KRAS participate to a significant gene network related to the Ras signalling pathway.
source: Archaic introgression at these genomic regions was first confirmed by Signet analysis, with TBC1D1 and PRKAG2 being included in a significant gene network belonging to the AMPK signalling pathway, while RASGRF2 and KRAS participate to that related to the Ras signalling pathway (Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results

claim: EPAS1 is a member of a significant network belonging to the Pathways in cancer.
source: The same analysis pointed to EPAS1 as a member of a significant network belonging to the Pathways in cancer, a complex group of biological functions such as those involved in Ras, MAPK, VEGF, and HIF-1 signalling cascades (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000; Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1f)
evidence: Supported by Signet analysis results shown in Figure 3A

claim: There is a link between biological mechanisms activated within hypoxic tumour microenvironments and those involved in high-altitude adaptations.
source: These findings emphasize a link between biological mechanisms activated within the context of hypoxic tumour microenvironments in different types of cancers and those involved in high-altitude adaptations, especially as concerns functions that might underlie the improved angiogenesis observed in Tibetan and Sherpa individuals (Gnecchi-Ruscone et al., 2018; Calderón - Gerstein and Torres - Samaniego, 2021)
evidence: Inferred from the functional pathway analysis and supported by citations

claim: Accumulation of HIF-1α transcriptional factor in the nucleus of cells close to hypoxic tumour masses comports the activation of diverse biological responses such as the formation of dense capillary structures.
